If making window.name read-only is possible I'm all for it. I'm pretty worried there will be some |if (!ie) {..}| code somewhere that breaks when other UAs change it though.

@zetafunction Thank you for the test link again, and sorry for the lag.

It does look like IE doesn't propagate .name sets from inside a subframe to the browsing context name.  Though I'm not sure what to make of those last two testcases, where it doesn't propagate `.name` sets on the `<iframe>` itself either, right?

I also tried a test sort of like http://jsfiddle.net/wcjLnbxx/ in IE (not that exact one because for some reason in that exact one I don't see any alerts in IE; my version of it had the iframe source in a separate same-origin file) and it looks like the property remains an accessor even after the set; it's just not propagated to the browsing context.

Given this, I do think it may be worth making window.name not propagate to the browsing context in subframes....

@bzbarsky I just noticed a flaw in my test methodology: IE was ignoring the `<script>` blocks...

I updated the "from child window.name" case to account for this (http://ithildin.com/tests/window/name.html, http is important), and now I get some results that I'm not sure how to interpret: the names set by window.name can be targeted by hyperlink navigations, but they are not accessible as named properties of window, same origin or not.

That's exciting.

Well, sounds like setting .name at least needs to target hyperlink navigations no matter what...

Hi, anyone here? Chrome has bug depending on this issue and needs speedy spec decision.
Can someone summarize the current behavior of different browsers in the various situations here?

With http://ithildin.com/tests/window/name.html IE11 opens the first four links inside the `<iframe>`s and the last four in a new window. For that page, only when the name is set on an `<iframe>` (rather than `window.name`) is it accessible in IE11. Origin does not seem to matter.

Firefox opens all links inside the `<iframe>`, Chrome only the first six. The rest is the same as OP.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/544
@shhnjk no, see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/257#issuecomment-148711081.
I think @annevk wrapped up current behavior of different browsers. Shall we start deciding the spec?
@annevk would you be able to prioritize this? Chrome would really like to implement something here according to the spec.
@domenic it's not clear to me what I need to here since it's not clear what we want to preserve and what we want to drop.
Chrome stating what they'd like to implement would help, since it seems browser behavior is all over the map.

My impression is that Chrome would like to just have any well-defined spec that all browsers are agreed to converge on; given divergent behavior across browsers there should be no need to preserve any of Chrome's existing semantics. But @shhnjk may have more specific opinions.

So I guess we have these options:
1. Have separate slots for frame names and window names. This appears to be what Edge does. If the frame name is the empty string, it's corresponding window name is used as frame name. And vice versa. Frame names (including when inherited from window names) pollute the global scope. Window names are used by hyperlinks.
2. Avoid polluting the global scope with names not known to the global. This is the Firefox model. We only expose names of cross-origin frames on the global if those names match the current value of the name attribute of the frame.
3. Whatever Safari/Chrome do. They appear to match each other, but they also seem to make little sense.

The Edge model still leaks due to the inheritance. The Firefox model leaks due to a frame being able to influence the properties of its parent. The Safari/Chrome model leaks all over as far as I can tell.

Preferences? Personally I think that based on this Firefox makes the most sense.

(I don't have a good answer for @shhnjk test in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/257#issuecomment-153981811. It appears that all browsers apart from Firefox are vulnerable. That very much has to do with "what names are in scope" when navigating and we don't really have a good model there yet I think.)

It seems option 2 would be best option among them. And regarding my test, we can do same using "opener" so I don't know if anyone cares but having option 2 will eliminate this problem isn't it? If so, 2 might be best option for security but I don't know if that breaks any website or not.
@shhnjk how does 2 address which name a hyperlink targets? I'm not sure I follow that.

I thought Firefox is not vulnerable to cross-origin hyperlink targets because it does not pollute global scope with names not known to the global. That's why I thought implementing option 2 will solve cross-origin hyperlink targets but I might be wrong.

I think this bug is only about what named properties get exposed on a given global.

There's a different bug (probably several at this point) as to which "browsing context names" are scoped together and are available to navigation from a particular place. I think your testcase falls in this category as the named properties on a given global are only concerned with children, not opener and such.
Hmm I got it. Anyways, my opinion is for option 2.
